clinicalPearls: A third nerve palsy with pupil involvement is a compressive palsy until proven otherwise, classically from a posterior communicating artery aneurysm
The eye is typically down and out with ptosis, and a dilated poorly reactive pupil signals external compression of the superficial pupillomotor fibres
Sudden painful pupil-involving third nerve palsy demands urgent vascular imaging to exclude a life-threatening aneurysm
Pupil-sparing complete palsies in older vasculopathic patients are more often ischaemic (microvascular), but this reassurance applies mainly to complete palsies
Aberrant regeneration (for example lid elevation on adduction) points to a chronic compressive or traumatic rather than ischaemic cause
Any progressive, incomplete or evolving palsy warrants imaging even if the pupil is initially spared
reference.pathophysiology: The pupillary parasympathetic fibres travel superficially on the oculomotor nerve and derive their blood supply from surface vessels, so external compression (from an aneurysm, tumour or uncal herniation) tends to involve the pupil early. In contrast, microvascular ischaemia from diabetes or hypertension damages the central fascicles while sparing the peripheral pupillomotor fibres, producing a pupil-sparing palsy. Compression of the nerve as it passes near the posterior communicating artery or through the cavernous sinus and superior orbital fissure accounts for the classic anatomical patterns.
additionalDifferentials: Cavernous sinus or superior orbital fissure lesion
Midbrain (fascicular or nuclear) third nerve lesion
Ocular myopathy or thyroid eye disease
additionalInvestigations: Urgent CT or MR angiography to exclude an aneurysm
MRI of the brain and cavernous sinus for compressive or infiltrative lesions
Assessment of pupil, lid and full ocular motility
Vasculopathic risk-factor evaluation when ischaemia is considered
Acetylcholine-receptor antibody testing if myasthenia is possible
redFlags: Pupil involvement, especially with acute severe pain
Signs of raised intracranial pressure or reduced conscious level
Progression or additional cranial nerve involvement
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the cause; microvascular palsies commonly recover over weeks to a few months, whereas compressive palsies depend on timely treatment of the underlying lesion, and a ruptured aneurysm is life-threatening.
pitfalls: Falsely reassuring pupil sparing in an incomplete or evolving palsy
Delaying angiography in a pupil-involving palsy
Attributing the palsy to diabetes without imaging when features are atypical
Missing aberrant regeneration that indicates a chronic compressive cause
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
